analysis.one_liner: Extends bank-style anti-money-laundering recordkeeping and reporting rules to crypto exchanges, wallets, miners, and kiosks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended, despite bipartisan sponsorship and three committee hearings.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would treat many crypto companies and even individual network participants—exchanges, wallet providers, miners, and bitcoin ATM operators—as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act. That means keeping records, filing reports, and flagging suspicious activity to federal regulators, just as banks do. It also adds rules targeting tools used to hide transactions, such as mixers and privacy coins, and requires bitcoin ATMs to verify customer identity. The aim is to make it harder to use cryptocurrency for scams, ransomware payments, drug money, and sanctions evasion.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who are the main victims of crypto scams, ransomware, and fraud: law enforcement would get the same paper trail on crypto that it has long had on bank transfers, making it easier to trace stolen funds and catch operators of fraudulent schemes. Consumers using bitcoin ATMs would get identity checks that make theft and fraud harder.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes digital asset providers and facilitators financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, requiring them to keep records, file disclosures, and report suspicious activity to aid detection of money laundering and terrorist financing [S2].
It requires U.S. persons with more than $10,000 in digital assets in foreign accounts to file a report, matching the offshore reporting requirement banks already face [S2] [S3].

Digital asset kiosk operators would have to verify each customer's identity with government-issued ID, collect counterparty information, and update the physical addresses of their machines every 90 days [S2] [S3].

Treasury would have to issue rules requiring financial institutions to control risks from mixers, privacy coins, and other anonymity-enhancing technologies—tools commonly used to conceal ransomware and fraud proceeds [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cryptocurrency exchanges, wallet providers, miners, validators, and bitcoin ATM operators would bear new registration, recordkeeping, monitoring, and reporting costs. Ordinary crypto users would face more identity collection and less transactional privacy, and some self-hosted wallet users and developers could see their activity swept into regulated territory.

drawbacks.text: The bill defines regulated financial institutions to include unhosted wallet providers, miners, and validators—participants who in many cases cannot actually identify the parties to the transactions they process, which critics said makes the compliance obligations technically infeasible [S3].
The bill's focus on mixers and anonymity-enhancing technologies, and its reach over self-hosted wallets, would reduce financial privacy for ordinary users who are not involved in any crime [S3].

Broad regulation of U.S. digital asset participants could push development and trading activity offshore, where it would be harder for U.S. regulators to see at all—a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the enforcement gains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea—applying money-laundering rules that banks have followed for decades to an industry where scams and ransomware flow freely—has a solid public-interest case. But the bill is drafted broadly: it sweeps in miners, validators, and self-hosted wallet software that often cannot comply, risks pushing the industry offshore, and trades away some privacy for law-abiding users. A narrower bill targeting exchanges, kiosks, and custodial services would have captured most of the benefit at a fraction of those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee held three hearings on digital assets but never voted on the bill or sent it to the full Senate, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, joined by Sens. Roger Marshall, Joe Manchin, and Lindsey Graham, giving it unusual bipartisan sponsorship for crypto legislation [S1] [S3].
Nineteen senators cosponsored: 16 of 48 Senate Democrats, 2 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 4 Senate independents [S4].

The bill was referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which held hearings on digital assets in October 2023, January 2024, and February 2024, but never marked up or voted on the bill [S5].
No version of the bill ever received a floor vote in either chamber, and no companion bill passed the House, so the bill expired with the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cryptocurrency firms avoided new Bank Secrecy Act reporting and registration obligations, and the unhosted wallets, mixers, and kiosks through which fraud and ransomware proceeds often move remained outside the recordkeeping regime. Consumers who fall victim to crypto scams gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crypto firms that avoided reporting rules

industries.industry: Cryptocurrency exchanges and custodial wallet providers
industries.note: They would become financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, with registration, recordkeeping, and suspicious-activity reporting duties similar to banks. Their resistance to these obligations runs against consumers, who bear the losses when crypto fraud and hacks go untraceable.

The bill would designate miners, validators, and other network participants as financial institutions, imposing compliance duties on actors who do not hold customer funds. Their interest in avoiding oversight runs against the public's interest in traceable transactions.

They would face 90-day address reporting, government-ID verification of every customer, and counterparty information collection. Unregistered kiosks have been linked to fraud and drug-money laundering, so their resistance runs against consumers targeted by those scams.

Treasury would have to require financial institutions to control risk from mixers and anonymity-enhancing technologies, which could effectively cut these services off from the banking system. Their interest in transactional anonymity conflicts with law enforcement's ability to follow fraud and ransomware proceeds.
